Hi Sam — thanks for the clear ask. High level options we can offer that map to your three points: 

1) Optional Capacity Zones — reserve a baseline across a set of US zones (region-level baseline) with a single committed rate. You only pay the committed baseline (monthly) whether you use it or not; burst is billed separately.

2) Rate Stabilization Guardrail — for the first 6 months we can cap the per-token/usual unit rate for the committed baseline (and step it up at pre-agreed intervals thereafter). This gives you predictability while we observe your new workload.

3) Burst Credits + True-up Window — include a bucket of burst credits (3 months of expected peak) that replenish on renewal, plus a 60-day true-up window to reconcile consumption vs commit. If consumption is below baseline we offer partial crediting to the next quarter (not a full refund).

I attached a one-page summary that shows an example 12-month structure with a baseline, burst credits and a 10% introductory discount on the baseline for months 1–3. If you like, we can convert this to a DocuSign during the call.

Next steps I propose: 1) internal review w/ finance (I will loop in our pricing lead), 2) numeric example run using your Q1 usage (attached), 3) 30-min sync to finalize term structure.

Best,
Rohan Mehta

+1 on the structure overall. A couple of guardrails / edits from finance/legal: 

- Make the 10% intro discount limited to the baseline invoice only (explicitly exclude burst billing).
- Change the underusage credit to a "carry-forward credit" capped at 25% of the next quarter's baseline for accounting simplicity. We prefer not to create multi-period liabilities.
- Add a commit floor clause: if customer reduces baseline by >25% mid-term, we require a 60-day notice and a one-time adjustment fee equal to 5% of the remaining committed value. This protects inventory and slot allocation.

If you can accept those edits I think we can approve the concession. Also recommend adding a short clause in the SOW that enumerates which zones are in the "Optional Capacity Zone" (explicit naming avoids confusion).

Ben Carter
